Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

High

Hackers Spied on a Stock Exchange Executive's Outlook Mailbox for Five Months

The Hacker News
2026-06-04 14 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Unknown attackers spent at least five months inside the Outlook mailbox of a senior executive at a major global stock exchange, copying the inbox out in small, repeated batches and routing it through Dropbox and OneDrive so the traffic blended into normal cloud activity. Symantec and Carbon Black's Threat Hunter Team reported the campaign this week. This points to espionage, not a money grab:

ATT&CKT1053.005 T1190 T1195.002 T1528 T1555.003 T1566
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Spied on a Stock Exchange Executive's Outlook Mailbox for Five Months
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Aspose.Email/Aspose.Pst mailbox library loaded by non-Outlook process · [LLM] Scheduled task masquerading as Adobe/Lenovo/OneDrive system service · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] FRPC (Fast Reverse Proxy client) execution by config-file argument
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PST exported by non-Outlook binary with password and date-range CLI flags · [LLM] curl/non-browser binary uploading to Dropbox or OneDrive personal API endpoints · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] Aspose.Email/Aspose.Pst mailbox library loaded by non-Outlook process Installation High
Hunts for the Aspose .NET library — which the Symantec/Carbon Black report identifies as the core of the attacker's mailbox stealer — being loaded by any process other than legitimate Outlook utilities. Aspose.Email and Aspose.Pst are the modules that read OST and write PST; their use outside Outlook/scanpst is highly anomalous on an executive endpoint. Rationale: Aspose.Email/Aspose.Pst are the specific libraries the article names as the heart of the mailbox stealer; loading them outside Outlook/scanpst is high-fidelity. Cross-checked Aspose product naming on the vendor site and Symantec's WastedLocker/Cl0p style write-ups, which use the same library identifiers. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.aspose.com/email/net/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1114/001/
ATT&CKT1114.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has_any ("Aspose.Email", "Aspose.Pst") or FolderPath has_any ("Aspose.Email", "Aspose.Pst")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("outlook.exe", "scanpst.exe", "scanost.exe", "olmapi32.dll")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
WindowsEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 7
| where EventData has_any ("Aspose.Email", "Aspose.Pst")
| where EventData !has "OUTLOOK.EXE" and EventData !has "scanpst.exe" and EventData !has "scanost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Provider, EventID, EventData
title: Aspose Mailbox Library Loaded by Non-Outlook Process
id: 5c7d2e3a-9b4f-4a12-bd1a-1c2e3f4a5b6c
description: Detects Aspose.Email or Aspose.Pst .NET libraries being loaded by a process other than Outlook or PST repair tools, a signature behaviour of the stock-exchange-executive mailbox stealer reported by Symantec.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hackers-spied-on-stock-exchange.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/04
tags:
  - attack.collection
  - attack.t1114.001
  - attack.t1005
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ImageLoaded|contains:
      - 'Aspose.Email'
      - 'Aspose.Pst'
  filter_legit:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\outlook.exe'
      - '\scanpst.exe'
      - '\scanost.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
  - Third-party mail-archive / e-discovery tools (Veritas, MailStore) that legitimately use Aspose
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:7 (@ImageLoaded:(*Aspose.Email* OR *aspose.email* OR *Aspose.Pst* OR *aspose.pst*)) -@Image:(*\\outlook.exe OR *\\OUTLOOK.EXE OR *\\scanpst.exe OR *\\scanost.exe)
#event_simpleName=ClassifiedModuleLoad OR #event_simpleName=ImageHash
| ImageFileName=/(Aspose\.Email|Aspose\.Pst)/i
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\\(outlook|scanpst|scanost)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, ImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name!=outlook.exe Processes.process_name!=scanpst.exe Processes.process_name!=scanost.exe (Processes.process IN ("*Aspose.Email*","*Aspose.Pst*") OR Processes.parent_process IN ("*Aspose.Email*","*Aspose.Pst*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name!=outlook.exe Processes.process_name!=scanpst.exe Processes.process_name!=scanost.exe (Processes.process IN ("*Aspose.Email*","*Aspose.Pst*") OR Processes.parent_process IN ("*Aspose.Email*","*Aspose.Pst*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
[LLM] PST exported by non-Outlook binary with password and date-range CLI flags Actions on Objectives High
Detects file writes of .pst files by a process that is not Outlook/scanpst when the launching command line carries password or date-range arguments. This is the article-specific operational pattern: the attacker's Aspose-wrapped tool was 'run each time with a password and a date-range flag' to slice the mailbox into bi-weekly chunks. Rationale: Both the file shape (.pst created by a non-Outlook process) and the CLI argument shape (password + date range) come directly from the article's description of how the attacker ran the tool eight times between Nov 2025 and Feb 2026. The combination is what makes it high-fidelity — either signal alone is too noisy. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1114/001/
ATT&CKT1114.001 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".pst"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("outlook.exe", "scanpst.exe", "scanost.exe", "olmapi32.dll")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-password", "/password", "-pwd", "/pwd", "-startdate", "-enddate", "/startdate", "/enddate", "-from", "-to", "-range", "/range", "-since")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".pst"
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("outlook.exe", "scanpst.exe", "scanost.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-password", "/password", "-pwd", "/pwd", "-startdate", "-enddate", "/startdate", "/enddate", "-from", "-to", "-range", "/range", "-since")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
title: PST Export by Non-Outlook Binary with Password and Date-Range Flags

references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

[LLM] Scheduled task masquerading as Adobe/Lenovo/OneDrive system service Installation Medium
Hunts for schtasks.exe /create operations naming the task after Adobe, Lenovo or OneDrive when the parent process is not the corresponding genuine installer/updater. The Symantec write-up explicitly calls out scheduled tasks 'posing as Adobe, Lenovo and OneDrive system services' as the persistence layer. Rationale: The article explicitly names Adobe, Lenovo and OneDrive as the three vendors the attacker impersonated in scheduled-task names. Combining the schtasks /create command with those exact brand strings and a non-vendor parent process produces an article-specific pivot rather than a generic schtasks rule. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036/005/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/create", "-create")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Adobe", "Lenovo", "OneDrive")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("setup.exe", "msiexec.exe", "AdobeARM.exe", "Adobe_Updater.exe", "AdobeUpdateService.exe", "OneDriveSetup.exe", "OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe", "LenovoUpdate.exe", "SystemUpdate.exe", "trustedinstaller.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Adobe" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)\Adobe" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Microsoft OneDrive" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Lenovo"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/create", "-create")
| where CommandLine has_any ("Adobe", "Lenovo", "OneDrive")
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\setup.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\msiexec.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\AdobeARM.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\OneDriveSetup.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\LenovoUpdate.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\trustedinstaller.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName
title: Scheduled Task Masquerading as Adobe/Lenovo/OneDrive Service
id: 8a1b2c3d-4e5f-4a6b-9c1d-3e4f5a6b7c8d
description: Detects schtasks.exe /create commands whose task name impersonates Adobe, Lenovo, or OneDrive system services when the parent is not the corresponding vendor installer - matches the persistence masquerade in the Symantec stock-exchange espionage report.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hackers-spied-on-stock-exchange.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/04
tags:

  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/create'
      - '-create'
  selection_name:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'Adobe'
      - 'Lenovo'
      - 'OneDrive'
  filter_legit_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\setup.exe'
      - '\msiexec.exe'
      - '\AdobeARM.exe'
      - '\OneDriveSetup.exe'
      - '\OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe'
      - '\LenovoUpdate.exe'
      - '\trustedinstaller.exe'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_name and not filter_legit_parent
falsepositives:

level: medium
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*\/create* OR *-create*) @CommandLine:(*Adobe* OR *Lenovo* OR *OneDrive*) -@ParentImage:(*\\AdobeARM.exe OR *\\OneDriveSetup.exe OR *\\OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe OR *\\LenovoUpdate.exe OR *\\trustedinstaller.exe OR *\\msiexec.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(\/|-)create/i
| CommandLine=/(Adobe|Lenovo|OneDrive)/i
| NOT (ParentBaseFileName=/^(setup|msiexec|AdobeARM|Adobe_Updater|OneDriveSetup|OneDriveStandaloneUpdater|LenovoUpdate|trustedinstaller)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

[LLM] FRPC (Fast Reverse Proxy client) execution by config-file argument Command & Control Medium
Hunts for execution of frpc.exe or any renamed binary running with the distinctive FRPC config-file argument pattern. Symantec's published indicator set explicitly lists FRPC as the tunneling tool used in the intrusion kit alongside the mailbox stealer. Rationale: FRPC is named outright in the Symantec indicator bundle. Its config file is canonically frpc.ini (or .toml in newer builds) — covering both the binary name and the config-arg pattern catches renamed-binary variants used to evade naive name-only rules. Cross-checked against the public fatedier/frp GitHub repo for argument conventions. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/fatedier/frp • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "frpc.exe"
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("frpc.ini", "frpc.toml", "frpc.yaml")
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s+-c\s+\S*frpc\.(ini|toml|yaml)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\frpc.exe"
    or CommandLine has_any ("frpc.ini", "frpc.toml", "frpc.yaml")
    or CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s+-c\s+\S*frpc\.(ini|toml|yaml)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: FRPC Fast Reverse Proxy Client Execution

[LLM] curl/non-browser binary uploading to Dropbox or OneDrive personal API endpoints Actions on Objectives High
Detects curl, wget or other non-browser executables making outbound connections to Dropbox API hosts or OneDrive personal endpoints. Matches the article's exfiltration mechanic — the attacker pulled a Dropbox API token, uploaded with curl, and used OneDrive Personal to blend into normal cloud traffic. Rationale: The article explicitly names curl + Dropbox API tokens for the exfil channel and OneDrive Personal as the alternative. Pairing those destinations with non-browser process initiators (which never legitimately need to hit personal-cloud APIs on a corporate executive's workstation) yields a tight, article-specific detection. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1567/002/ • https://www.dropbox.com/developers/documentation/http/documentation
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl.exe", "wget.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe", "rclone.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.dropboxapi.com", "content.dropboxapi.com", "files.dropbox.com", "dropboxusercontent.com", "onedrive.live.com", "storage.live.com", "my.microsoftpersonalcontent.com")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("api.dropboxapi.com", "content.dropboxapi.com", "Authorization: Bearer", "Dropbox-API-Arg")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SrcUsername != ""
| where DstHostname has_any ("api.dropboxapi.com", "content.dropboxapi.com", "files.dropbox.com", "dropboxusercontent.com", "onedrive.live.com", "storage.live.com")
| join kind=inner (
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessName in~ ("curl.exe", "wget.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe", "rclone.exe")
        or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("api.dropboxapi.com", "content.dropboxapi.com", "Dropbox-API-Arg")
) on $left.DvcHostname == $right.DvcHostname
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.

DeviceProcessEvents

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "5926b86b642e00672252953eb30d8f75cfb7797fe3118bd6fa2cfbee92905d61", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "82d83274680df928fdda296a348e01802f595e412308c399565c320df444052a", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "8bf051251ec3b973e39a313547e53421a2f8d2f6", "608d01124cd6b5b8c55888e984b4c4d9b06fa686", "ab9903d9edc720d1e11ea7d3d3e7a1c456f44ff7") or SHA1 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "5926b86b642e00672252953eb30d8f75cfb7797fe3118bd6fa2cfbee92905d61", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "82d83274680df928fdda296a348e01802f595e412308c399565c320df444052a", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "8bf051251ec3b973e39a313547e53421a2f8d2f6", "608d01124cd6b5b8c55888e984b4c4d9b06fa686", "ab9903d9edc720d1e11ea7d3d3e7a1c456f44ff7") or MD5 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "5926b86b642e00672252953eb30d8f75cfb7797fe3118bd6fa2cfbee92905d61", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "82d83274680df928fdda296a348e01802f595e412308c399565c320df444052a", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "8bf051251ec3b973e39a313547e53421a2f8d2f6", "608d01124cd6b5b8c55888e984b4c4d9b06fa686", "ab9903d9edc720d1e11ea7d3d3e7a1c456f44ff7")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "5926b86b642e00672252953eb30d8f75cfb7797fe3118bd6fa2cfbee92905d61", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "82d83274680df928fdda296a348e01802f595e412308c399565c320df444052a", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "8bf051251ec3b973e39a313547e53421a2f8d2f6", "608d01124cd6b5b8c55888e984b4c4d9b06fa686", "ab9903d9edc720d1e11ea7d3d3e7a1c456f44ff7"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Jupyter Enterprise Gateway /api/kernels POST with KERNEL_* YAML-injection payload Exploitation Medium
Hunts for HTTP POSTs to the Jupyter Enterprise Gateway `/api/kernels` endpoint whose body carries `KERNEL_WORKING_DIR`, `KERNEL_POD_NAME`, `KERNEL_NAMESPACE` or other `KERNEL_*` env values containing YAML-injection markers (`---`, `...`, embedded `securityContext`, `runAsUser`, `privileged`). This is the exact CVE-2026-44182 exploit shape — the unsanitised env-var is interpolated into the Jinja2 pod manifest at kernel-pod.yaml.j2 line 77 and lets the caller overwrite or append Kubernetes resources. Rationale: Anchors on the exact exploit primitive from the GHSA PoC: a POST to /api/kernels carrying KERNEL_WORKING_DIR/KERNEL_POD_NAME/KERNEL_NAMESPACE whose value embeds a YAML breakout (`\n# INJECTION\n securityContext:\n runAsUser: 0` or `...\n---\napiVersion: v1\nkind: Pod`). The Jinja2 line referenced (kernel-pod.yaml.j2#L77) and the launch_kubernetes.py uppercase→lowercase conversion (lines 130-137) confirm these are the only attacker-controlled fields. No second-source corroboration searched — single advisory CVE. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-cfw7-6c5v-2wjq
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1611
Data sourcesWeb.Web
// Endpoint-tier visibility only — looks for outbound connections from a host to the EG service
// where the EG ingress is reachable internally; pair with WAF/ingress body inspection in Sentinel.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (31529, 8888, 8889, 8443)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/kernels" or AdditionalFields has "/api/kernels"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Detects KERNEL_* env-var with YAML-injection markers in EG application syslog or WAF body logs.
// CommonSecurityLog does NOT carry DeviceName — use DestinationHostName / SourceIP for host pivots.
let InjectionMarkers = @"(?i)KERNEL_[A-Z_]+[^\n]{0,200}(---|\.\.\.|securityContext|runAsUser|runAsGroup|fsGroup|privileged\s*:\s*true)";
union isfuzzy=true
(
  Syslog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where ProcessName has_any ("enterprise_gateway", "enterprise-gateway", "jupyter") or SyslogMessage has "/api/kernels"
  | where SyslogMessage matches regex InjectionMarkers
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="Syslog", Host=Computer, HostName, ProcessName, Evidence=SyslogMessage
),
(
  CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where RequestURL has "/api/kernels" and RequestMethod =~ "POST"
  | where Message matches regex InjectionMarkers or DeviceCustomString1 matches regex InjectionMarkers or AdditionalExtensions matches regex InjectionMarkers
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="WAF/Proxy", Host=DestinationHostName, SourceIP=SourceIP, ProcessName=DeviceProduct, Evidence=coalesce(Message, DeviceCustomString1, AdditionalExtensions)
),
(
  W3CIISLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where csUriStem == "/api/kernels" and csMethod =~ "POST"
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="IIS", Host=Computer, SourceIP=cIP, ProcessName="w3wp", Evidence=strcat(csMethod, " ", csUriStem, "?", csUriQuery)
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Privileged or root pod created by Jupyter Enterprise Gateway ServiceAccount Installation High
Detects the Kubernetes-API-server-side effect of CVE-2026-44182: a Pod created by the enterprise-gateway ServiceAccount whose spec contains `privileged: true`, `runAsUser: 0`, `runAsGroup: 0`, a `hostPath` mount, or `hostNetwork: true`. EG should only ever spawn unprivileged kernel pods running as uid 1000 (jovyan); any privileged spec from this SA is the post-injection footprint. Rationale: Anchors on the EG-default identity (the `enterprise-gateway` ServiceAccount, see Helm chart) and the article-stated effects: the PoC explicitly produces pods with `privileged:true, runAsUser:0, runAsGroup:0` and notes the impact extends to arbitrary `hostPath` mounts. Normal EG kernel pods run as `uid=1000(jovyan)` per the rendered template — any privileged/root spec from this SA is the injection footprint, not noise. Only the original GHSA cross-checked. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-cfw7-6c5v-2wjq • https://github.com/jupyter-server/enterprise_gateway/blob/152c20f162f2fab700c04c8830ebf8c1e2e2217a/etc/kernel-launchers/kubernetes/scripts/kernel-pod.yaml.j2#L77 • https://github.com/jupyter-server/enterprise_gateway/blob/152c20f162f2fab700c04c8830ebf8c1e2e2217a/etc/kernel-launchers/kubernetes/scripts/launch_kubernetes.py#L130-L137

title: Privileged Pod Created by Jupyter Enterprise Gateway ServiceAccount (CVE-2026-44182)
id: 7e2a9c4b-1d8f-4a3e-9b6c-5f0a8d2e1c7f
description: Detects pod creation by the enterprise-gateway ServiceAccount whose spec contains privileged true, runAsUser 0, hostNetwork true, hostPID true, or a hostPath volume — the post-exploitation footprint of CVE-2026-44182 Jinja2 YAML injection.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-cfw7-6c5v-2wjq
  - https://github.com/jupyter-server/enterprise_gateway/blob/152c20f162f2fab700c04c8830ebf8c1e2e2217a/etc/kernel-launchers/kubernetes/scripts/kernel-pod.yaml.j2#L77

logsource:
  product: kubernetes

detection:

level: high
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:create @objectRef.resource:pods @stage:ResponseComplete @user.username:*enterprise-gateway* (@requestObject.spec.securityContext.runAsUser:0 OR @requestObject.spec.securityContext.runAsGroup:0 OR @requestObject.spec.containers.securityContext.privileged:true OR @requestObject.spec.hostNetwork:true OR @requestObject.spec.hostPID:true OR @requestObject.spec.volumes.hostPath.path:*)

           or @message like /"hostNetwork":true/
           or @message like /"hostPID":true/
           or @message like /hostPath/)
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 200

[LLM] Jinja2 SSTI payload to Jupyter Enterprise Gateway /api/kernels (CVE-2026-44181) Exploitation High
Hunts for HTTP POST requests targeting Jupyter Enterprise Gateway's /api/kernels endpoint carrying a Jinja2 server-side template injection payload in KERNEL_POD_NAME / KERNEL_WORKING_DIR / KERNEL_NAMESPACE fields. Specifically pivots on the Python sandbox-escape gadgets (cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen, __subclasses__, __builtins__) that the PoC and any real-world weaponization must include to reach OS-command execution. Rationale: All keywords (`/api/kernels`, `KERNEL_POD_NAME`, `KERNEL_WORKING_DIR`, `KERNEL_NAMESPACE`, `{{`, `cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen`, `__subclasses__`) are taken verbatim from the GHSA PoC. The combination of an EG endpoint URL plus Jinja2 mustache markers plus Python globals-walk gadgets has essentially zero benign explanation. Defender XDR cannot inspect inbound HTTP bodies, so defender_kql is empty by design; Falcon FDR likewise does not ship raw HTTP body content. CloudWatch is non-applicable (not AWS-specific telemetry). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f49j-v924-fx9w • https://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings/blob/master/Server%20Side%20Template%20Injection/Python.md
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006

[LLM] Enterprise Gateway service account creates privileged / hostPath / RBAC-escalating pod (CVE-2026-44181 post-exploit) Actions on Objectives High
Hunts for Kubernetes API actions by the Jupyter Enterprise Gateway service account that fall outside its legitimate role of launching kernel pods: creating a pod with privileged securityContext, hostPath / hostNetwork / hostPID, or creating/updating rolebindings, clusterrolebindings, or reading cluster secrets. These are the textbook pivots after stealing the EG SA token via SSTI RCE, as the GHSA explicitly notes. Rationale: The GHSA explicitly enumerates the Enterprise Gateway SA's RBAC — including `pods [create]`, `secrets [get watch list]`, `rolebindings [create]` — and explicitly names the attacker's next step (schedule a privileged pod or hostPath-volume pod for cluster takeover). The detection ties three article-specific anchors together: actor identity (`enterprise-gateway` in the SA username), action verb (create/update on pods/rolebindings/secrets), and payload shape (`privileged:true`, `hostPath`, `hostNetwork`, `hostPID`) — the legitimate kernel-launcher YAML never includes any of those. Falcon LogScale is left empty because FDR does not ship K8s audit; Defender Advanced Hunting likewise has no K8s-audit table. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f49j-v924-fx9w • https://github.com/jupyter-server/enterprise_gateway/blob/152c20f162f2fab700c04c8830ebf8c1e2e2217a/etc/kernel-launchers/kubernetes/scripts/kernel-pod.yaml.j2
ATT&CKT1611 T1078.004 T1552.005

[LLM] Enterprise Gateway python container spawns shell or reads K8s service-account token (CVE-2026-44181 RCE) Installation High
Hunts for the on-host signal of the SSTI RCE landing inside the Jupyter Enterprise Gateway pod: a python interpreter spawning a shell, recon binary, or curl/wget, or any process reading /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. The article's PoC uses `cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('hostname')` — `os.popen` results in a python→sh→hostname process tree that is otherwise unheard-of for the EG service. Rationale: The PoC payload `cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen("hostname").read()` proves the exact process-tree shape the detection targets: python (the Enterprise Gateway service) → sh -c → hostname. The article also explicitly names theft of the Kubernetes service-account token (`/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token`) as the attacker objective, so we additionally pivot on any python-parented process referencing that path. Host-scope filters (`enterprise-gateway` in hostname / pod name / container image) keep the signal tight to the vulnerable workload rather than every python process in the fleet. CloudWatch is empty (not CloudTrail/VPC-flow telemetry). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f49j-v924-fx9w • https://github.com/jupyter-server/enterprise_gateway/blob/152c20f162f2fab700c04c8830ebf8c1e2e2217a/enterprise_gateway/services/processproxies/k8s.py#L219-L247
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1552.005

[LLM] Jupyter Enterprise Gateway /api/kernels POST with KERNEL_UID/GID body (CVE-2026-44180) Exploitation Medium
Hunts inbound POST requests to /api/kernels on the Enterprise Gateway service that supply KERNEL_UID or KERNEL_GID in the JSON body — the attack surface used to exploit the prohibited-UID/GID whitespace bypass described in CVE-2026-44180. Most production workloads call /api/kernels without explicitly setting these env keys, so unsolicited UID/GID-bearing requests are high-signal. Rationale: Anchors on the exact attack-surface URL '/api/kernels' and HTTP POST method from the PoC. Body content (the '0 ' bypass payload) rarely makes it into access logs, so this UC is a coarse hunting pivot — pair with UC2 (K8s audit on runAsUser=0) for ground truth. Cross-checked GHSA-chq7-94j8-cj28 and Jupyter Enterprise Gateway upstream docs (jupyter-enterprise-gateway.readthedocs.io kernel-envs). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-chq7-94j8-cj28 • https://jupyter-enterprise-gateway.readthedocs.io/en/latest/users/kernel-envs.html • https://github.com/jupyter-server/enterprise_gateway/blob/main/etc/kernel-launchers/kubernetes/scripts/kernel-pod.yaml.j2

[LLM] Enterprise Gateway service account creates Jupyter kernel pod as root (CVE-2026-44180 outcome) Exploitation High
Detects the post-exploitation footprint of CVE-2026-44180: a Kubernetes pod-create call whose service account belongs to enterprise-gateway and whose resolved PodSpec has runAsUser=0 or runAsGroup=0. Default kernel pods run as jovyan (1000:100); any kernel-* pod created with root UID/GID is either the documented bypass or a misconfiguration that should never reach production. Rationale: Article confirms the default kernel pod runs as uid=1000(jovyan) gid=100(users) — any kernel pod from the enterprise-gateway SA with runAsUser=0 is exactly the bypass outcome (Jinja2 int-coerces '0 '→0 even when EG_PROHIBITED_UIDS rejects '0'). Cross-referenced the kernel-pod.yaml.j2 template at jupyter-server/enterprise_gateway main branch (where securityContext.runAsUser is templated from KERNEL_UID). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-chq7-94j8-cj28 • https://github.com/jupyter-server/enterprise_gateway/blob/main/etc/kernel-launchers/kubernetes/scripts/kernel-pod.yaml.j2 • https://jupyter-enterprise-gateway.readthedocs.io/en/latest/users/kernel-envs.html

[LLM] Jupyter kernel pod created with hostPath volume by enterprise-gateway SA Actions on Objectives High
Detects the container-escape vector named in the advisory: a kernel pod from the enterprise-gateway service account that mounts a hostPath volume — especially sensitive worker-node paths (/, /etc, /var/spool/cron, /root, /home, /var/run/docker.sock). Combined with the root UID bypass (UC2), this is the path to crontab-driven node compromise the PoC describes. Rationale: The advisory explicitly names the escape recipe: 'use a hostPath R/W volume mount, use this UID/GID bypass to run as root, and then gain code execution in the underlying worker node by creating a crontab entry'. Kernel pods normally do not need hostPath at all — the default kernel-pod.yaml.j2 ships with only emptyDir-style mounts. Any hostPath volume on a kernel-* pod from the EG SA is article-defined-malicious. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-chq7-94j8-cj28 • https://github.com/jupyter-server/enterprise_gateway/blob/main/etc/kernel-launchers/kubernetes/scripts/kernel-pod.yaml.j2
ATT&CKT1611 T1610
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb == "create"
| where tostring(ObjectRef) has "\"resource\":\"pods\""
| where tostring(User) has "enterprise-gateway" or Username has "enterprise-gateway"
| extend req = todynamic(tostring(RequestObject))
| extend podName = tostring(req.metadata.name)
| extend volumes = req.spec.volumes
| mv-expand v = volumes
| extend hostPath = tostring(v.hostPath.path)
| where isnotempty(hostPath)
| extend sensitive = iff(hostPath in ("/", "/etc", "/root", "/home", "/var/spool/cron", "/var/run/docker.sock", "/var/lib/kubelet", "/proc")
                          or hostPath startswith "/etc/"
                          or hostPath startswith "/var/spool/cron"
                          or hostPath startswith "/root/", "sensitive", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, podName, hostPath, sensitive, User, AuditId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Cron/persistence file written on Kubernetes worker node from container runtime context Installation Medium
Detects creation or modification of /etc/cron* or /var/spool/cron/* files on Kubernetes worker nodes — the article's explicit post-escape persistence vector after the CVE-2026-44180 UID bypass + hostPath mount. Kernel pods exist to run user code, not to schedule host-level cron jobs; any cron-file write on a worker node is investigation-worthy. Rationale: Article PoC explicitly recommends 'creating a crontab entry in the mounted host file system' as the worker-node escape outcome. Filters specifically on container-runtime-spawned writes (runc / containerd-shim) because legitimate cron edits on a K8s worker should come from configuration-management agents (cloud-init, Ansible, Puppet) or package installs — not from runc. Cross-checked the article's mount-namespace escape pattern against MITRE T1611 / T1053.003. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-chq7-94j8-cj28 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611/
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1611

     or FolderPath == "/var/spool/cron"
     or FolderPath startswith "/var/spool/cron/"
     or (FolderPath == "/etc" and FileName in ("crontab","anacrontab"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where OSPlatform in ("Linux","Ubuntu","RedHat","CentOS","Debian","SUSE")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/run/containerd","/var/lib/docker","/var/lib/containerd","/usr/bin/runc","/usr/sbin/runc")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("runc","containerd-shim","containerd-shim-runc-v2","crun","kata-runtime")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("runc","containerd-shim","containerd-shim-runc-v2","crun")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

     or TargetFilePath in ("/etc/crontab","/etc/anacrontab")

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45247")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45247")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:

            - '\powershell.exe'

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

level: high

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

Autonomous AI Tool Finds 2-Year-Old RCE Flaw in Redis (CVE-2026-23479)

The Hacker News
2026-06-03 8 use cases 5 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Redis has patched a use-after-free in its blocking-client code that lets an authenticated user run arbitrary OS commands on the machine hosting the database. The flaw was found by an autonomous AI tool built to hunt bugs in large codebases. Tracked as CVE-2026-23479, the flaw was introduced in Redis 7.2.0 and remained in every stable branch until the May 5 fixes, unnoticed for over two years.

CVEsCVE-2026-23479

[LLM] Redis-server process spawning shell or scripting interpreter (CVE-2026-23479 RCE) Exploitation High
Hunts the terminal stage of the CVE-2026-23479 exploit chain: the use-after-free in unblockClientOnKey() ultimately repoints strcasecmp() to system() via a GOT overwrite, so the next Redis command is executed as a shell command. Any child process of redis-server that is a shell, scripting interpreter, or download tool is a high-fidelity indicator of in-the-wild exploitation. Rationale: Article describes that the GOT overwrite repoints strcasecmp() to system(), so 'the next command Redis parses runs as a shell command.' That child shell will be parented to redis-server in EDR telemetry — an extremely rare event in any legitimate Redis deployment. No second source needed: the parent-child relationship is a direct consequence of the published exploit chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/redis-cve-2026-23479-uaf • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-23479
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("redis-server","redis-server.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "/redis-server"
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\redis-server.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wget","curl","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
imProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName endswith "/redis-server" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\redis-server.exe" or ParentProcessName =~ "redis-server" or ParentProcessName =~ "redis-server.exe"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/ksh","\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","/wget","/curl","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/python","/python3","/perl","/ruby","/php")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
